passage: Jomon, twenty, stood outside the only tailor's shop in Thodupuzha holding two shirt fabrics and his phone. He had already sent photos to four friends. "Hansa, blue or green?" he called to his cousin, who was buying rice across the road. "Blue," she said. A friend texted "green" a minute later, and Jomon's stomach sank. At the co-op bank where he'd just started as a clerk, the manager had called his ledger "a bit untidy", and he had lain awake all night replaying it. Hansa crossed over. "Which one do you like?" Jomon opened his mouth. Nothing came. "I... don't know." "Then stand here till you do," she said, smiling. "No phones." It took four minutes. Green.

qa.q: How many friends had Jomon sent photos to?
qa.a: He had sent photos to four friends.

qa.q: Why did Jomon's stomach sink when a friend texted "green"?
qa.a: The different opinion made him unsure and anxious, because he relies on others' approval to decide.

qa.q: What small step did Hansa suggest, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She asked what he liked and told him to decide without phones, a small chance to trust his own judgement.

qa.q: How might Hansa see Jomon's habit of asking everyone?
qa.a: She seems fond of him but aware he has lost touch with his own preference, so she nudges him kindly.

grounding: A young man in a small town seeks opinions before a simple choice and is crushed by mild criticism, and his cousin nudges him to find his own view.

passage: In a shared flat in Malmö, Tomas, twenty-one, rewrote his university essay introduction for the fifth time. He'd already asked his flatmate Ulla, his mum and two classmates if it was okay. Ulla said it was fine but "a bit long". For the rest of the evening Tomas barely spoke, feeling like a failure. When his mum replied "Brilliant!", he felt great for about ten minutes, then began doubting again. Around midnight Ulla found him still at the kitchen table. "What do you think of it?" she asked. "I don't know. That's the problem." "Try this. Read it out loud and tell me one thing you're proud of in it. Just you." He read. "The last line. I like the last line." "Good. Start there."

qa.q: How many times had Tomas rewritten his introduction?
qa.a: He rewrote his essay introduction for the fifth time.

qa.q: How did Tomas feel after Ulla said the essay was "a bit long"?
qa.a: He felt crushed and like a failure, barely speaking for the rest of the evening.

qa.q: What turning point did Ulla offer, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She asked him to name one thing he was proud of on his own, which starts building his own sense of worth instead of borrowing it.

qa.q: How might Ulla feel seeing her mild comment upset Tomas so much?
qa.a: She may feel surprised and a little guilty, but she stays kind and helps him look inward.

grounding: A student whose mood rises and falls with others' approval begins, with a flatmate's help, to find his own judgement of his work.
